title: Panaetius softens the porch
hook: Panaetius brought Stoicism to Rome and made it more humane for ordinary people

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Chrysippus, who gave the school its structure. Your line was the builder. This week: Marcus's blind spots, his themes, your notebook, the Meditations closed, then Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus.
screen: `THE BUILDER.` → `A WEEK: MARCUS CLOSES, THE PORCH OPENS.`

segments.voice: Some gyms post a photo of a champion by the door: this is the goal. Others post a sign: you showed up, that counts. Both want you stronger. Only one makes a beginner want to come back. The early Stoics talked a lot about the sage, the perfectly wise person, and admitted that almost nobody had ever been one. That's a hard poster to walk past every day. Then a philosopher from the island of Rhodes carried the school to Rome and quietly changed the sign on the door. Today: kathēkon.
screen: `A CHAMPION'S PHOTO, OR "YOU SHOWED UP"?` → `THE SAGE: ALMOST NOBODY.` → `PANAETIUS CHANGES THE SIGN.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Panaetius of Rhodes spent years in Rome among the circle of Scipio Aemilianus, a leading general and statesman, and later became head of the Stoic school in Athens. Later writers credit him with helping Stoicism take root in Rome. Second, the change. Earlier Stoics drew a sharp line: the sage is wise, everyone else is a fool, and there's nothing in between. Panaetius, as later writers report him, cared about the people in between, those making progress. He wrote about duties for ordinary life: how a decent person acts as a citizen, a friend, a family member, in their own particular role. Third, the word. His book was called On Appropriate Action; the Greek is kathēkon, what's fitting for you to do. Cicero later rebuilt it into a Latin book, On Duties, coming up in a few days. And Panaetius taught that each person has their own nature, too: not everyone should try to live the same life. Fourth, why it mattered. He didn't throw out the high ideal. He made a path toward it that ordinary people could walk. A senator, a soldier, a parent could do the fitting thing today without being a sage. Looking back over the week: Zeno's vision, Cleanthes' praise, Chrysippus's structure, and now Panaetius, making a door more people could walk through.
screen: `RHODES TO ROME.` · `FOR THE PEOPLE IN BETWEEN.` · `KATHĒKON: WHAT'S FITTING FOR YOU.` · `A PATH ORDINARY PEOPLE COULD WALK.` · then, large: `GENTLER FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Think of one practice you keep failing at because the bar is set too high: twenty minutes of meditation, never getting angry, reading every day. Size it, the Panaetius way, for a real person in your real life: twenty minutes becomes two, never angry becomes one pause. Let your shoulders drop as you choose the gentler version.
Kathēkon. Panaetius's word for the fitting action, what's appropriate for you to do; Cicero later translated it as duty. Today's word.
Your line: gentler for everyone. The high ideal stays; the door just gets wider. That's a week, from Marcus to the porch.

original.note: Greek: what's fitting, the appropriate action. Panaetius's subject; Cicero translated it into Latin as officium, duty.

notes: Panaetius c. 185–110/109 BC; with Scipio Aemilianus in Rome; head of the Stoa after Antipater of Tarsus (c. 129 BC). Confirm.
Attention to the prokoptōn (one making progress): attested mainly via Seneca, Letters 116.5, and Cicero. Hedged with 'as later writers report him'; confirm.
Each person's own nature (the four personae): Cicero, On Duties 1.107–117. Confirm attribution to Panaetius.
'Middle Stoa' is a modern label; confirm wording.
